blocks.title: Bond energy
blocks.text: The bond energy is the average amount of energy required to break all bonds of a particular type in one mole of a substance. It is determined experimentally by measuring the heat involved in a chemical reaction, and its unit is kJ per mol.

Bond energy is a measure of the strength of a bond and its reactivity. The strength of a bond depends on the electronegativity difference of the bonded atoms and on the size of the atoms. In the H-X compounds, where X is F, Cl, Br or I, the bond energy rises with increasing electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms: as the difference increases the bond polarity becomes greater, which gives rise to an additional attractive force binding the atoms. This is why the bond energy of HF (565 kJ per mol) is higher than that of HI (295 kJ per mol). The energies of multiple bonds are greater than those of single bonds: C triple bond C > C=C > C-C.

blocks.title: Bond length
blocks.text: Bond length is the distance between the nuclei of two atoms forming a covalent bond. It is determined experimentally by physical techniques such as electron diffraction, X-ray diffraction or spectral studies.

The bond length is governed by many factors, including electronegativity, size and the nature of the covalent bond (single, double or triple). With an increase in the size of the atoms the covalent bond length increases: the C-Cl bond is about 180 pm whereas C-F is 135 pm, because the chlorine atom is much larger. With a rise in electronegativity difference between the bonded atoms the bond is shortened: the Si-F bond length in SiF4 is found to be near 155 pm, whereas calculation from the covalent radii of Si (117 pm) and F (64 pm) gives 181 pm. The electronegativity difference gives the covalent bond an ionic character, and the extra attraction between the bonded atoms shortens the bond.

blocks.long_description: The H-X bond energy falls from HF to HI as the electronegativity difference, and so the polarity, decreases. Multiple bonds between the same atoms are stronger and shorter than single bonds. Larger atoms give longer bonds (C-F to C-I), and a bigger electronegativity difference gives a shorter bond, as in Si-F at 155 pm against 181 pm from the covalent radii. The lower chart shows the ionic bond strongest, then covalent, then metallic, with hydrogen bonds, dipole-dipole and London forces far weaker.
